Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

64.4% of Iowa's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 64.4% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $1,040 a year ($87 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $696 and $1,370. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $696 · Typical $1,040 · A quarter pay over $1,370 · A tenth pay $1,873 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 4,984 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $1.9 billion of building and $521.5 million of contents coverage across all Iowa policies.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 14,788 NFIP flood claims and $346.2 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2008, 2019 and 1993.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2008 ($160,257,152), 2019 ($26,751,131), 1993 ($26,182,604). Total paid $346,167,462. Totals for the latest two years are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

That is 14,788 claims since 1978 against 9,431 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 18.4% of the 3,374 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 3,374 policies reporting one)18.4%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)36.1%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 11,348 claims paid with a damage figure)12.7%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Why do sites quote different prices for Iowa?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $1,040 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $970; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

47.4% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $820, full-risk $966 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$820
  • Median full-risk premium$966
  • Pay below full-risk47.4% of 4,984

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $2,000 (44.4% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways to lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Building deductibleShare of policies
$1,25023.5%
$1,5007.8%
$2,00044.4%
$5,00013.7%

Single-family primary homes; the commonest deductibles. Your lender may limit how high you can go.

Elevated vs not elevated is not what raising your home would save: the two groups sit in different zones and places, so compare like with like on your own quote.

  • Median premium, elevated buildings$742 (406 policies)
  • Median premium, not elevated$825 (4,578 policies)

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 8,834 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 111 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Repeat-flood damage records8,834
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)111

These count damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes. How this is counted

How often is Iowa a flood disaster?

54 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storms and Flooding (2026).

  • 2026 — Severe Storms and Flooding
  • 2024 — Severe Storms, Flooding, Straight-Line Winds, and Tornadoes
  • 2024 — Severe Storms, Tornadoes, and Flooding
  • 2023 — Flooding
  • 2019 — Severe Storms and Flooding
  • 2019 — Severe Storms and Flooding

Only the latest are listed, newest first, one line per disaster; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $244.1 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $4,461 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.
